title: Helix overrides Kitty Terminal's `cursor_trail` configuration
body:
<!--
Your enhancement may already be reported!
Please search on the issue tracker before creating a new issue.
If this is an idea for a feature, please open an "Idea" Discussion instead.
-->

I'm using Helix on macOS through the Kitty terminal emulator with the `cursor_trail` feature enabled. My kitty.conf is configured as follows:

```conf
cursor_trail 10
cursor_trail_decay 0.1 0.3
```

This configuration allows the cursor to have a trail effect similar to that of **Neovide**.

When I use Neovim within Kitty, the cursor trail effect works as expected because Neovim does not override Kitty's cursor settings.

However, when I use Helix, the cursor trail effect does not take effect. It appears that Helix's internal mechanisms override Kitty's cursor configurations.

**Expected Behavior**

Helix should respect the terminal emulator's cursor settings, allowing the cursor trail effect to function as configured.

**Possible Solutions**

Is there a way to prevent Helix from overriding the terminal emulator's cursor effects, or can this be configured through existing settings? If not, could this feature be added in a future update?

**Environment**

Operating System: macOS 14.7.2
Terminal Emulator: Kitty 0.39.0
Helix Version: 25.01.1 (e7ac2fcd)

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: this is not possible, we always overwrite the terimnals cursor because we support multiple cursor and the terminal only supports a single cursor

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
kitty.conf

```
cursor_shape block
cursor_trail 1
cursor_trail_decay 0.1 0.3
cursor_trail_start_threshold 0
shell_integration no-cursor
```

.config/helix/config.toml

```toml
[editor.cursor-shape]
insert = "bar"
normal = "underline"
select = "underline"
```

Edit: switched normal and select mode to underline for easier distinction. Thank me later.

comments.body: @participant2 Interesting, for some reason only the block shape doesn't work.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body:
I believe this is because the block shape does not use the same block character as a shell. Helix simply inverts the background of what is under the cursor.

For the other shapes like underline, helix has to print the underline character and kitty can latch on.

comments.author: participant4
comments.body:
Not sure how much a plugin will be able to override the way the cursor is rendered.
It's way simpler to add a cursor type in addition to the exiting `block`, `beam` and `underline`. Something like `native_block`, to make the distinction with the default emulated block cursor.

This way, the default remain the same, with hight level of customization with theme, but with a possibility for those that needs it (for accessibility reason for example) to use a less themable but terminal compatible cursor.

For those interested, someone made this PR that is doing it: https://github.com/helix-editor/helix/pull/13821

You can see that it is very small change. While doing it in a plugin will probably be way more complex.

comments.author: participant6
comments.body:
Apologies for commenting on an unplanned issue, but I've implemented a draft solution that I'll be testing over the coming days.
I added a `use_terminal_cursor` config option that uses the terminal's native cursor instead of Helix's software-rendered cursor (when only a single cursor is active). The changes are relatively small and it works well with Ghostty shaders.

> Note: In my current draft, the default is set to true for easier testing. This should be changed to false before any potential merge to maintain backward compatibility.

Happy to open a PR if there's interest once I've finished testing.

comments.author: participant7
comments.body:
I submitted a PR: https://github.com/helix-editor/helix/pull/16151

- I duplicated `CursorKind::Block` into `BlockSoftware` and `BlockHardware`, as @participant4 suggested. I defined a serde attribute to avoid breaking existing config files declaring cursors as `block`.
- `BlockSoftware` behaves exactly the same as `Block` used to.
- `BlockHardware` follows almost the same code path as `BlockSoftware` but it does not hide the terminal cursor, which renders on top of the primary software cursor. When the hardware cursor needs to be elsewhere (e.g. when typing a command or a search regex) the software cursor underneath takes over. Because of this, it's a good idea to select a theme with primary cursor colors matching the terminal cursor colors.

Sample config:
```
[editor.cursor-shape]
insert = "block-hardware"
normal = "block-hadrware"
select = "block-hardware"
```

I believe this PR could be merged, maybe after some minor revisions.
- It provides a hardware block cursor, but unlike the PRs previously linked here it does *not* replace the existing software block cursor. Instead, the users have the option to select the hardware block cursor in their configuration.
- It does not add any new logic and mostly relies on existing code. It is unlikely to contribute tech debt or maintainance burden.

Please let me know what you think 🙏
